title: Which central elements are transitive? An answer to a question of Campion Loth and Rattan on Jucys–Murphy evaluations
oneLine: Transitive Jucys–Murphy images fill the symmetric-group centre exactly when (n−1)! is invertible, with optimal degree 2n−2; over the complex numbers every central element is the transitive image of one symmetric function.
abstract: The Jucys–Murphy elements of the symmetric group are sums of transpositions, and by theorems of Jucys and of Murphy the symmetric polynomials in them give exactly the centre of the group algebra, even over the integers. Expanding such a polynomial produces products of transpositions whose counts are Hurwitz-type numbers. Keeping only the transitive products, those whose transpositions connect all n letters, defines the transitive image T_n(f); Goulden and Jackson, and Campion Loth and Rattan, showed that it is central, and Campion Loth and Rattan asked which subalgebra of the centre these images generate (their Question 12). This candidate shows that over the complex numbers no generation is needed: every central element is the transitive image of a single symmetric function. Over an arbitrary commutative ring, the transitive images span the centre, and also generate it as a unital algebra, exactly when (n−1)! is invertible; when they span it, every central element has a preimage of degree at most 2n−2, and this degree cannot be lowered. The pairs consisting of an ordinary and a transitive evaluation of the same function are exactly the pairs of central elements with equal coefficients at the n-cycles. Over the integers a conjugation-orbit argument bounds the image classwise; an exact, degree-free computation shows that this bound describes the integral image exactly for n ≤ 5 and n = 7 but not for n = 6, where the image has index 2, and that adding the scalars closes the image under multiplication for n ≤ 7. Limits: the integral description is complete only for n ≤ 7, the n = 6 parity condition is unexplained, and closed forms for classical bases are not addressed. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 3.2 (proof, main): T_n maps the symmetric functions over R onto the centre Z(R𝔖_n) if and only if (n−1)! is a unit in R; over every R the identity coefficients of transitive images form exactly (n−1)!R; over ℂ every central element is a single transitive image, answering Question 12 of Campion Loth and Rattan.

Theorem 4.1 (proof, main): when (n−1)! is a unit, every central element is T_n(f) with deg f ≤ 2n−2, and no symmetric function of smaller degree has a transitive image with nonzero identity coefficient.
Theorem 5.1 (proof): when (n−1)! is a unit, the pairs (E_n(f), T_n(f)) are exactly the pairs of central elements with equal coefficients at the n-cycles.

Proposition 6.1 and Theorem 6.2 (proof): products of transitive images have K_λ-coefficients divisible by z_λ/h_λ; the unital algebra they generate is the whole centre only when (n−1)! is a unit, and for each prime p ≤ n−1 the p-cycle class stays out of reach modulo p.

Theorem 6.3 (exact computation): the integral image equals the classwise lattice L_n for n ≤ 5 and n = 7, has index 2 in L_6 with one explicit parity condition, and together with the scalars is closed under multiplication for every n ≤ 7.

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about shuffles, swaps and connected factorisations.

The symmetric group is the group of all shuffles of a set of objects. Its centre consists of the combinations of shuffles that do not depend on how the objects are labelled. Jucys–Murphy elements are particular sums of swaps, and plugging them into symmetric polynomials produces exactly this centre, a classical theorem of Jucys and of Murphy. Expanding gives products of swaps, whose counts are Hurwitz-type numbers that also count branched covers of the sphere.

Often only connected products matter: those whose swaps link all the objects together. Keeping only these gives the transitive image. Goulden and Jackson, and then Campion Loth and Rattan, showed that it is still central, and Campion Loth and Rattan asked which part of the centre these connected versions produce.

This candidate answers the question. Over the complex numbers, every central element is the connected version of a single symmetric function. Over a general number system, this works exactly when n minus one factorial can be divided by; otherwise even products of connected versions fall short. When it works, degree two n minus two is enough, and no smaller degree reaches the identity. Over the integers, an orbit-counting bound describes the image exactly for up to five objects and for seven, but not for six, where one extra parity condition appears.

The key idea is an inclusion–exclusion formula over ways of splitting the objects into groups, which turns each Jucys–Murphy element into a plain number, so the group sizes can be read off.

There are limits. The integer description is complete only up to seven objects, by exact computation, and the parity condition at six is not yet understood.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and exact computation rather than by peer review, and this briefing uses a synthetic voice that is not additional evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Campion Loth and Rattan (2025), Centrality of star and monotone factorisations. Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society. Proves that transitive images of all symmetric functions are central and asks (Question 12) which subalgebra they generate.

Goulden and Jackson (2009), Transitive powers of Young–Jucys–Murphy elements are central. Journal of Algebra. Centrality of transitive powers, with an inclusion–exclusion argument for star factorisations.
Féray (2012), Partial Jucys–Murphy elements and star factorizations. European Journal of Combinatorics. A conceptual proof of the Goulden–Jackson centrality through partial permutations.
Jucys (1974), Symmetric polynomials and the center of the symmetric group ring. Reports on Mathematical Physics. Symmetric polynomials in the Jucys–Murphy elements give the centre, over the integers.

Murphy (1983), The idempotents of the symmetric group and Nakayama's conjecture. Journal of Algebra. Theorem 1.9: the centre over any integral domain is the ring of symmetric polynomials in the Jucys–Murphy elements.
Murray (2004), Generators for the centre of the group algebra of a symmetric group. Journal of Algebra. A secondary account of the integral Jucys–Murphy theorem and its generators.

Coulter, Do and Moskovsky (2025), Integration on complex Grassmannians, deformed monotone Hurwitz numbers, and interlacing phenomena. Canadian Journal of Mathematics. Cited in a closing remark as a family to which the Möbius formula applies; no claims are made about it.
